en: Abhidhānottara, Chapter 9:
The Chapter on the Ritual for the Classification of All Non-Abiding Karmas (IX. *Sarvānaṣṭhitakarmabhedavidhānapaṭala*) from Kalff’s 1979 thesis.
Now I shall further explain the ritual procedure for the Solitary Hero (Ekavīra). The practitioner of mantra should contemplate [the deity] at the navel, situated in the midst of wind and fire.

Above that is a double-petaled lotus (*viśvapadma*) upon a solar disc, with a skull-cup filled with the nectar of the five wisdoms; in its center, the vowels and consonants are doubled in both forward and reverse order.

Having empowered himself with the syllable HŪṂ through the yoga of Vajrasattva, he should meditate on himself as the glorious Heruka, who has become the bliss of supreme joy—four-faced, twelve-armed, and standing in the *ālīḍha* posture.

His face is formidable with fangs, he has three eyes and a distorted countenance; he tramples upon the head of Bhairava and Kālarātri; he is clothed in a tiger skin and is radiant with the play of the aesthetic flavor of compassion.

With his two arms embracing Vajravārāhī, he holds a five-pronged *kalāpa* vajra and a vajra-bell; with his other two arms, he wears the skin of Gaṇapati as his garment. In his third right hand is a vajra-spear, in the fourth a hook (*aṅkuśa*), in the fifth a vajra-knife (*karttikā*), and in the sixth a vajra-drum (*ḍamaruka*). In his third left hand is a skull-cup (*kapāla*) filled with human flesh (*arjaparipūrṇa*).

[42b3] Full with the application of the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*), the vajra-khaṭvāṅga has five upward-pointing prongs, from which hang a *kalāpa* vajra-bell and various multicolored banners. In the center, it is marked with a double-vajra (*viśvavajra*). Below, there is a single-pronged vajra; in the fourth position, a vajra-noose; and in the fifth, a Brahma-head. In the sixth, an axe. It has faces that are blue, yellow, white, red, and green, with expressions of fierce laughter, passion, heroism, disgust, and licking. Before him stand Āli and Kālī, and the Blessed Lady Vajra-...

Vārāhī is red in color, four-faced, four-armed, and three-eyed; her hair is disheveled, she is naked, and she wears a girdle adorned with fragments. Her left arm embraces [the consort], and she holds a skull-cup.

With the blood of the wicked Māra and so forth filling her right hand with the *bodhicitta*, she holds a threatening forefinger, a vajra, and a flaying knife (*karttikā*). In her other two hands, she holds a *ḍamaru* drum and a *khaṭvāṅga*. She is fond of flowing blood, resembling the fire at the end of an aeon (*kalpāgni*).

Her two legs are poised in the posture of great bliss and compassion. She is red, green, yellow, and blue, with a face that is fierce, terrifying, and formidable; her facial colors are purified in accordance with those of the Blessed One.
[43a4] (m) The color of the arms [is to be understood] from the painting.

Having thus arranged the sequence of the sacred seats (pīṭha) and so forth, one should perform the supreme self-yoga: PUṂ is on the head for Khaṇḍakapālin and Pracaṇḍā; JĀṂ is at the crest-lock (śikhā) for Mahākaṅkāla and Caṇḍākṣī.
OṂ || Kaṅkālaprabhāvatī is at the right ear. AṂ || Vikaṭadaṃṣṭriṇīmahānāsā is at the spine; this is the seat (pīṭha). GOṂ || Surāvairiṇīvīramatī is at the left ear.
RĀṂ || Between the eyebrows is Amitābhakharvarī. DEṂ || From the two eyes is Vajraprabhalaṅkeśvarī. MĀṂ || From the roots of the arms is Vajradehadrumacchāyā. This is the *upapīṭha*.
Khecarī is at the mind-wheel; KĀṂ. Airāvatī with Aṅkurikā is at the two armpits; OṂ. Vajrajaṭilā and Mahābhairavā are at the pair of breasts; KṢETRAṂ.
TRIṂ: At the center of the navel is Mahāvīravāyuvegā. KOṂ: At the nose is Vajrahūṃkārasurābhakṣī. This is the *upakṣetra*. KAṂ: At the mouth is Subhadraśyāmādevī.

LAṂ at the throat: Vajrabhadra and Subhadrā; this is the *Chandoha*. KĀṂ at the heart: Mahābhairava and Hayakarṇā; HIṂ at the genitals: Virūpākṣa and Khagānanā; this is the *Upacchandoha*. Bhūcarī belongs to the wheel of speech (*vākcakra*).
PREṂ || At the sexual organ is Mahābalacakravegā. GRIṂ || At the anus is Ratnavajrakhaṇḍarohā.
The meeting place: SAUṂ. On the two thighs are Hayagrīva and Sauṇḍinī.

SUṂ: On the shank is Ākāśagarbha and Cakravarmiṇī; this is the Upamelāpaka. NAṂ: On the fingers is Śrī Heruka and Suvīrā. SIṂ: On the tops of the feet is Padmanarteśvara and Mahābalā; this is the Śmaśāna.
[44a2] MAṂ || Vairocanacakravartinī is at the two thumbs. KUṂ || Vajrasattvamahāvīryā is at the two knees. This is the secondary cremation ground (upaśmaśāna).
Pātālavāsinī belongs to the body wheel.
Ḍākinī is on the vajra; Lāmā on the bell; Khaṇḍarohā and Rūpiṇī on the elephant-hide and the fist; Kākāsyā on the vajra-spear; Ulūkāsyā on the goad.

Śvānāsyā holds a vajra-knife; Śūkarāsyā holds a hand-drum (ḍamaruka); Yamadāḍhī holds a skull-topped staff (khaṭvāṅga) with a skull-cup; Yamadūtī holds a noose (pāśa); Yamadaṃṣṭrī holds the head of Brahmā; and Yamamathanī holds an axe (paraśu).
The vessel of the mind of awakening is four-faced.
The earth element is Pātanī; the water element is Māraṇī; the fire element is Ākarṣaṇī; the wind element is Padmanarteśvarī; and the space element is Padmajālinī.
Vairocana is in the aggregate of form; Vajrasūrya is in the aggregate of feeling; Padmanarteśvara is in the aggregate of perception.
In the aggregate of formations (saṃskāraskandha) is Vajrarāja; in the aggregate of consciousness (vijñānaskandha) is Vajrasattva; and the reality (tattva) of all Tathāgatas is Śrī Herukavajra.
In the two eyes is Mohavajra; in the two ears is Dveṣavajra; in the two nostrils is Īrṣyāvajra; in the mouth is Rāgavajra; in touch is Mātsaryavajra; and in all the sense bases is Aiśvaryavajra.
Akṣobhya in the mind; Amitābha in speech; Vairocana in the body.
Oṃ haḥ, Vajrasattva is in the heart.
*Namaḥ* to the two *hi*s at the head is Vairocana; *svāhā* and *hūṃ* at the crest is Padmanarteśvara; *vauṣaṭ* and *he* on the two shoulders is Heruka.
HŪṂ HŪṂ HOḤ: Vajrasūrya at the two eyes. PHAṬ HAṂ: Paramāśvāstra on all limbs. OṂ VAṂ: Vajravārāhī at the navel. HĀṂ YOṂ: Yāminī at the heart.
*Hrīṃ moṃ* on the face is *Mohanī*; *hreṃ hrīṃ* on the head is *Saṃcālinī*; *hūṃ hūṃ* on the crest-lock is *Saṃtrāsanī*; and *phaṭ phaṭ* on all the limbs is the weapon (*astra*) of *Caṇḍikā*.

Having indeed placed the middle needle at the tip of the foremost knot, one should firmly apply the "thunderbolt of the thumb. Having positioned it at the center of the forehead, one should rotate it with a circling motion; then, with the feet stepped forward and the gaze directed upward, one should utter the *phetkāra* sound while facing upwards.

The heroes and yoginīs residing in the world-systems of the ten directions are summoned with *jaḥ hūṃ vaṃ hoḥ*. Having drawn them in by means of the vajra-hook and other mudrās, having caused them to enter, and having bound them, one should lead them [to the disciple]. Seeing the expanse of the sky filled with heroes and yoginīs, the arising of the empowerment for those two occurs through the gesture of bestowing empowerment from skull-cups filled with the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*).

"Just as all the Tathāgatas were bathed immediately upon birth, so shall I bathe [you] with pure, divine water. Oṃ sarvatathāgatābhiṣeka-samaya-śriye svāhā āḥ hūṃ. Upon the mandalas of wind and fire, there is a skull-cup arisen from the syllable ĀḤ, completely filled with the nectar of gnosis (jñānāmṛta), empowered by the sixteen digits and the syllable HŪṂ, and [consisting of] the three syllables.

One should meditate upon the three wheels as being truly pervasive. *Oṃ, all phenomena are pure by their very nature; I am pure by my commitment.* One should bring about a state of consciousness established in the equanimity of the single flavor of all phenomena. By means of the application of the nectar of gnosis, one should drink the water of the vajra-nectar: *Oṃ vajrāmṛtodaka hūṃ ṭha ṭha trāṃ āḥ khaṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā.*

Through the application of the mantra of gnosis, one should emanate the supreme tip of the wheel; thereafter, having performed the recitation with the great conch-bracelet, and having properly established the breath-control (prāṇāyāma) and meditated, it blazes forth at that very instant.
Oṃ śrīvajra he he ru ru ka hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ ḍākinījālasaṃvaraṃ svāhā. Oṃ hrīḥ ha ha hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ. These are the heart and near-heart mantras. Oṃ vajravairocanīye hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā.

Oṃ sarvabuddhaḍākinīye hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā. This is the heart-mantra and the near-heart-mantra of the Goddess. One should perform recitation and meditation in this manner until weariness arises. When weariness occurs, one should contemplate purification and abide in the thirty-seven factors conducive to enlightenment.
The application of mindfulness to the body is Ḍākinī.

The application of mindfulness to feeling is Lāmā; the application of mindfulness to phenomena is Khaṇḍarohā; the application of mindfulness to mind is Rūpiṇī; and she is the purity of the lotus of gnosis.

The base of psychic power of desire is Pracaṇḍā; the base of psychic power of energy is Caṇḍākṣī; the base of psychic power of investigation is Prabhāvatī; the base of psychic power of mind is Mahānāsā.

The faculty of faith is Vīramatī; the faculty of energy is Kharvarī; the faculty of mindfulness is Laṅkeśvarī; the faculty of concentration is Drumacchāyā. This is the purification of the mind wheel (cittacakra).
The faculty of wisdom is Airāvatī; the power of faith is Mahābhairavā; the power of vigor is Vāyuvegā; the power of mindfulness is Surābhakṣī.
The power of concentration is Śyāmādevī; the power of wisdom is Subhadrā.
Hayakarṇā is the factor of awakening that is concentration; Khagānanā is the factor of awakening that is vigor. This is the purification of the wheel of speech.
Cakravegā is the factor of enlightenment of joy; Khaṇḍarohā is the factor of enlightenment of tranquility.
The awakening-factor of discrimination of phenomena is Sauṇḍinī; the awakening-factor of mindfulness is Cakravarmiṇī; the awakening-factor of equanimity is Suvīrā; right view is Mahābalā.
Right intention is Cakravartinī; right speech is Mahāvīryā; the purity of the body wheel is [the third].
Right action is Kākāsyā.
Right livelihood is Ulūkāsyā; right effort is Śvānāsyā; right mindfulness is Śūkarāsyā. The four gates of liberation are as follows: right concentration is Śrī Heruka.
"I am one whose essential nature consists of the wisdom of the utterly pure dharmadhātu. This is the adamantine resolve (*yamadāḍhī*) for the production of wholesome dharmas that have not yet arisen.
The protection of wholesome states that have arisen is Yamadūtī; the abandonment of unwholesome states that have arisen is Yamadaṃṣṭrī.
The non-arising of unarisen unwholesome states is the Yamamathanī; this is the purification of the Samayacakra.
Thus, by cultivating this distinction, the practitioner will certainly achieve success; he whose nature is the union with the welfare of all beings is the supreme one of the pledge of equanimity.
One should meditate upon the fivefold wheels separately according to their distinct divisions; the womb-born is a separate division, the unsurpassed wheel of five.
One should meditate on the Lord of Yoginīs as divided into distinct parts; just as Heruka-Vajra is, so too is the Goddess in the center.
Surrounded by a yoginī through the yoga of the Buddha-Ḍākinī, one should visualize the heroes, such as Kāyavajra and the others, in the center of their bhagas.
Thus, by means of the yoga of the three wheels, one should meditate on the fivefold [deity] in sequence according to the meditation: in the bhaga, through the yoga of the ḍākinī in the center.
Through the yoga of Padmaḍākinī and by means of the differentiation of Vajraḍākinī, one should meditate upon the supreme Heruka within the three wheels in the center of the bhaga.
One should meditate upon him within the *samayacakra*s, in the maṇḍala of the *samayaḍākinī*s, by means of the application of the *jñānaḍākinī*, from the beginning, middle, and end of the universe.
Within the center of his own vulva, one should visualize the four wheels; there, one should visualize Heruka as the Solitary Hero, with the same color as Vārāhī.
One should visualize his face, arms, and weapons, as well as the universal lotus; then, in the center of that very bhaga, one should meditate upon the supreme Heruka.

One should meditate on that which consists of the fivefold [elements], joined with divisions and united with skulls; one should visualize it within the center of the *bhaga* according to the sequences of the Yoginī.
One should visualize the invisible wheel in the center of the *bhaga*; then, within the circle of heroes (*vīracakra*), one should perform meditation with the seal of embracing (*āliṅganamudrā*).
One should visualize the secret [mantra] in the heart of each respective Yoginī; the assembly consists of the Cakra-Yoginīs, resplendent with four arms.
Two hands are engaged in embracing, while the others hold various weapons; indeed, within their secret centers (bhaga) is the invisible contemplation of the Hero (vīrabhāvanā).

Through conventional means, one should practice the yoga of concealment; by means of the yoga of the egg-born sequence, one should meditate upon the supreme heroic visualization, which is invisible, through the process of analytical meditation.

One should meditate on the fifth [syllable] through the visualization of the supreme egg-born [deity], having divided it according to the differentiation of the wheel, just as in the visualization of yoga.

Meditation is according to the particularity of one's inclination and according to one's preference; the visualizations are distinguished by differences such as the dominant factor and by differences in family.
The manifestation of sovereignty is through the distinction of the various deities; having differentiated them by their distinct names, one should employ the term "ḍāka."
Alternatively, he exercises sovereignty through the distinction of the three bodies; through the distinctions of sovereignty and so forth, he will effect the division of the wheels.
According to the distinction of families, and by means of the various heroes and yoginīs of all [the deities], one should perform the meditation on the womb-born through the yoga of song.
The egg-born is devoid of song, free from both sound and non-sound; the self-arisen Blessed One is the most supreme among the distinctions of the unions of the sources.
Some yogins desire this, while other yogins do not; it is devoid of sounds such as song and established in the state of non-appearance.
The supreme state is unmanifest, sequential, and imperishable; it is subtle, devoid of the grasped and the grasper, and free from sounds such as those of song, yet it is the object of enjoyment.

Having enjoyed all the qualities of sensual pleasure for the benefit [of others], he, whose nature is compassion, exerted himself for the sake of all sentient beings with the most supreme patience and vigor.
The yogi does not find fault with song; it is beneficial for pleasing the ḍākinīs.
Hoḥ! May the essence of the three worlds be revealed to me.
A la la la hoḥ!
O Lord of Compassion, release your arrow; O Great Bliss, Victorious Sambhava!
A la la la hoḥ!
Release the essence that is difficult to perceive; it is the essence within the thousandfold self.
The union of Kāntā and Asura is the essence of the three worlds.
A la la la hoḥ!
The Suras, Ādhi, Sumuñca, Mahā, Chajina, and Mahāḥ— impelled by this,
the Protectors arise from the abode of the bliss of great bliss and should emit the entire assembly of Jinas of all the Buddhas.
In that which is partless, devoid of song, and free from the impurity of the egg-born, one perceives neither form there, nor pleasure, nor joy.
Free from duality, partless, and pure, it is the domain of that which is sung by conceptual construction; liberated from both dharma and adharma, it is not stained by sinful means.
Completely liberated from all dualities, the egg-born one is the supreme cultivation; the song of awakening from sleep cannot be faulted by the wise as being foolish.

One awakens through the meditations on the factors of enlightenment that are devoid of the welfare of sentient beings. Likewise, there is the goddess born of the field, the co-emergent goddess, and the yoginī born of the sacred seats.
The goddess born of the family, born of the mother, the invisible one, and likewise the sky-farer; she is born from the end, supreme, middling, and variously excellent.
She who moves upon the earth, she who belongs to the thirty [gods], and she who dwells in the depths of the underworld; likewise, the Yakṣinī, the Nāginī, the Gandharvī, and the Kinnarī.

The Apsarases who were perfected in the past, and others whose intentions are well-disposed toward the Sugata—those whose selves are deeply devoted to the Three Jewels—all of them are in the outer maṇḍala.
With various offerings for worship, and through the transformations of dance and song.
One should worship the Lord of the Ḍākinīs with various divine flavors; one should visualize the body-wheel as mounted upon the wind mandala.
One should instantly visualize the wheel of speech mounted upon the mandala of Varuṇa.
The wheel of mind, which brings about bliss, is mounted upon the mandala of fire; the supreme mandala of the pledge is mounted upon the mandala of Mahendra.
One should meditate upon the mandala of gnosis right there through the process of non-conceptualization; within the center of the bhaga-mandala, one should visualize a universal lotus.
One should visualize the Solitary Hero in the center of a solar disk; one should encircle the triple wheel with a garland of wheels, lotuses, and vajras.

Having encircled the wheel of the pledge (samayacakra) according to the ritual with a garland of crossed-vajras (viśvavajra), one should likewise encircle the outer mandala, since it consists of fivefold procedures.
Outside is a formidable cremation ground, possessing every color, most excellent of the excellent, delightful with various noble trees and terrifying with dogs and jackals.
There are crows, owls, wolves, vultures, cranes, and lizards; likewise, skeletons pierced by stakes are seen hanging there, half-burnt.
[The ground was covered] with skulls, hands, and heads, as well as headless trunks, various kinds of beautiful serpents, jackals, and frogs.
And by means of lions, boars, tigers, goats, and rams, as well as elephants, horses, donkeys, cows, camels, and various other excellent sacrificial animals.
With various kinds of supreme lotuses of the samaya, and with various kinds of supreme intoxicating drinks, one should drink.
The assembly of heroes is divine, consisting of various supreme yoginīs; they hold skull-bowls and khaṭvāṅgas in their hands, as well as excellent flaying knives and hand-drums (ḍamaru).

With various kinds of divine musical instruments, with the finest foods, snacks, and savory juices, and with diverse kisses and embraces, as well as the most excellent of things to be sucked and licked.
In such a cremation ground, one should offer an oblation right there to the yakṣas, vetālas, and rākṣasas, and should manifest the form of Heruka.
Playing the hand-drum, the vajra-bell, and performing music and dance, naked and joined with the mudrā, he utters "hūṃ phaṭ" and cries "kilakilā."
One should visualize the flame-mudrā by means of the ālīḍha posture; having filled the mouth with the pledge, one should thus recollect everything.
Oṃ āḥ arali hoḥ jaḥ hūṃ vaṃ hoḥ | Vajraḍākinīs, you are the samaya; behold, hoḥ!
In this manner, one should cause [the disciple] to recollect [this] three, four, or five times.
In forward and reverse order, with the skull-cups and those [offerings], one should recite the mantra with the vajra-añjali mudrā, [the hands] opened upwards.

Oṃ kha kha khāhi khāhi! May all yakṣas, rākṣasas, bhūtas, pretas, piśācas, unmādas, apasmāras, ḍākas, ḍākinīs, and so forth, accept this bali offering! Protect my samaya! Grant me siddhi! Eat, drink, and smell as you wish; do not transgress!
Be my companions for the sake of purifying true happiness in every way! Hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā!

In this manner, according to the prescribed ritual, one should cause it to be offered during the four junctions of the day; for the sake of the great purpose, in a secluded place well-established in comfort.
But by means of non-concentrated yoga, one should consume everything indeed.
Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Classification of All Non-abiding Karmas," in the illustrious *Abhidhānottara*.
